name: SSH & Remote Access
description: Key authentication, host verification, the config file, tunnels, agent forwarding and hardening a server.

modules.name: Keys, Trust & Config
modules.description: How SSH authenticates both directions, and how to make it pleasant to use.

cards.prompt: How does SSH public-key authentication work, and why is it better than a password?
cards.answer: You keep a private key; the server holds the public key in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. The server sends a challenge the client signs with the private key. The secret never crosses the network, so it cannot be phished, sniffed or brute-forced.
cards.explanation: Generate with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@host"` — Ed25519 is fast, short and the current default recommendation. Protect the key with a passphrase and let the agent cache it; permissions must be 600 on the private key or SSH refuses it.

cards.prompt: You get 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!'. What does it mean and what should you do?
cards.answer: The server's host key no longer matches `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. Either the server was rebuilt or rekeyed, or someone is intercepting the connection. Verify the new fingerprint through a separate trusted channel before removing the old entry.
cards.explanation: Host keys are how the *client* authenticates the *server* — the half people forget. Blindly running `ssh-keygen -R host` trains you to click through a genuine MITM. In fleets, publish host keys via configuration management or use SSH certificates.

cards.answer: Per-host aliases and defaults: `Host prod` with `HostName`, `User`, `Port`, `IdentityFile`, `ProxyJump` for bastions, and `ServerAliveInterval` to stop idle disconnects. Then `ssh prod` just works, and scp/rsync/git inherit it.
cards.explanation: `ProxyJump bastion` replaces fragile nested ssh commands. `ControlMaster auto` with `ControlPersist 10m` reuses one connection for subsequent sessions — dramatically faster for tools that open many SSH connections, such as Ansible.

cards.prompt: What is agent forwarding, and why is it risky?
cards.answer: It lets a remote host use your local agent to authenticate onward hops, without copying your key there. The risk is that anyone with root on that host can use the forwarded socket to authenticate as you while you are connected.
cards.explanation: Prefer `ProxyJump`, which tunnels the connection instead of exposing the agent. If you must forward, do it per-host rather than globally, and use `ssh-add -c` so each use requires confirmation.

modules.name: Tunnels & Hardening
modules.description: Port forwarding, file transfer and locking down sshd.

cards.answer: `-L` (local forward) opens a port on your machine that tunnels to a host reachable from the server. `-R` (remote forward) opens a port on the server that tunnels back to something reachable from your machine.

left.title: -L local:host:port
points: Reach a database behind a bastion

right.title: -R remote:host:port
points: Expose your local dev server outward

cards.explanation: `-D` adds a third mode: a local SOCKS proxy routing arbitrary traffic through the server. All three are legitimate admin tools and all three are also classic pivoting techniques — which is why forwarding is often disabled on hardened bastions.

cards.prompt: You need to sync a large directory to a server repeatedly over a flaky link. Which tool?
cards.answer: `rsync -avz --partial --progress` over SSH. It transfers only differences, compresses in flight, preserves metadata and can resume interrupted transfers — none of which scp does.
cards.explanation: Mind the trailing slash: `rsync src/ dst` copies the *contents*, `rsync src dst` copies the directory itself. Always dry-run with `-n` before adding `--delete`, which will happily mirror an accidental local deletion.

cards.prompt: How do you harden an internet-facing sshd?
cards.answer: Disable password authentication and root login (`PasswordAuthentication no`, `PermitRootLogin no`), allow only specific users or groups, use modern key types, rate-limit with fail2ban or firewall rules, and keep it behind a bastion or VPN where possible.
cards.explanation: Changing the port only reduces log noise — it is not security. The genuine wins are key-only auth and reducing exposure. Adding a hardware token (`sk-ed25519`) makes key theft alone insufficient.

cards.prompt: `git push` over SSH says 'Permission denied (publickey)'. How do you diagnose it?
cards.code:
$ ssh -T git@github.com
Permission denied (publickey).
$ ssh -vT git@github.com   # verbose: which keys were offered?
cards.answer: Run `ssh -vT` and read which identity files were offered. Usual causes: key not added to the agent (`ssh-add -l` is empty), wrong key for that account, key not registered on the host, or private-key permissions too open.
cards.explanation: SSH offers a limited number of keys before the server rejects the connection, so a crowded agent can fail even when the right key exists. Pin the key per host with `IdentityFile` plus `IdentitiesOnly yes`.

modules.name: Operating SSH at Scale
modules.description: Key management and the agent, SSH certificates, file-transfer protocols, persistent sessions and troubleshooting.

cards.prompt: Ed25519 vs RSA keys for SSH
cards.answer: Ed25519 is the modern default: small keys, fast, and resistant to implementation mistakes. RSA is universally supported but needs 3072+ bits today, and legacy `ssh-rsa` signatures using SHA-1 are disabled by modern OpenSSH.
cards.explanation: Use Ed25519 unless an old system forces RSA, and use a hardware-backed `ed25519-sk` key where possible so the private key cannot be copied off the device. Always set a passphrase; the agent makes that painless.

cards.answer: It holds decrypted private keys in memory so you type each passphrase once per session; `ssh` asks the agent to sign authentication challenges and the key itself never leaves it. `ssh-add` loads keys, `ssh-add -l` lists them, and `-t` sets a lifetime.
cards.explanation: OS integrations (macOS Keychain, Windows OpenSSH agent service, desktop keyrings, 1Password and similar) provide the agent automatically. Keep the loaded key set small — servers limit authentication attempts, so offering too many keys fails before the right one is tried.

cards.prompt: What problem do SSH certificates solve for a large fleet?
cards.answer: Instead of copying every user's public key into every server's `authorized_keys`, servers trust one certificate authority key. The CA signs short-lived user certificates (hours) carrying principals (allowed usernames) and restrictions; host certificates likewise remove "trust on first use" for host keys.
cards.explanation: Short-lived certificates make offboarding automatic — access expires rather than needing removal from hundreds of servers — and can be issued after SSO and MFA login. Tools such as HashiCorp Vault, Teleport and smallstep implement the CA workflow.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between scp, sftp and rsync over SSH today?
cards.answer: The legacy SCP protocol had design flaws (the remote side could influence which files were written), so modern OpenSSH's `scp` uses the SFTP protocol underneath by default. `sftp` is an interactive and scriptable file-transfer protocol. `rsync` transfers only differences and can resume.
cards.explanation: For one-off copies, `scp` is fine; for repeated or large syncs, rsync; for restricted file-only accounts, an SFTP-only user with `ForceCommand internal-sftp` and a chroot. Plain FTP sends credentials in cleartext and should not be used.

cards.prompt: You start a two-hour migration over SSH and your Wi-Fi drops. How should you have run it?
cards.answer: Inside a terminal multiplexer — `tmux` (or `screen`) — on the server, so the job keeps running when the connection drops and you can reattach (`tmux attach`). Alternatively run it as a proper service or job (`systemd-run`, a job queue). `nohup` survives the hang-up but loses the interactive session.
cards.explanation: A process started directly in an SSH session receives SIGHUP when the connection closes and usually dies mid-way. `mosh` keeps a roaming interactive session alive across network changes. Long operations belong in a multiplexer as a habit.

cards.prompt: Key authentication works for one user but not another on the same server, and the key is definitely in `authorized_keys`. What do you check?
cards.answer: Permissions: with `StrictModes` on, sshd ignores `authorized_keys` if the home directory, `~/.ssh` (should be 700) or the file (600) are writable by group or others. Also check ownership, SELinux contexts on the files, `AllowUsers`/`AllowGroups`, and the server log (`journalctl -u sshd` or `/var/log/auth.log`).
cards.explanation: The server log states the exact reason while the client only sees "Permission denied". `ssh -vvv` shows the client side; running `sshd -d -p 2222` in debug mode shows everything for a single test connection.

cards.prompt: To kill a frozen SSH session from the client side, press Enter, then type the escape sequence ___ .
cards.explanation: SSH escape sequences start with `~` at the beginning of a line: `~.` disconnects, `~^Z` suspends ssh, `~#` lists forwarded connections, `~C` opens a command line to add port forwards to a live session, and `~?` lists them all. When nested sessions are involved, `~~` sends a literal tilde to the inner one.
